payload.summary: Nestled in the sheltered crook of the Sølvfjord where the winter winds lose their teeth and the long summer light turns the meadows gold, Eyrby is the southern breadbasket of Hrafnland—a farming town of turf-roofed longhouses, stone-walled fields, and barley terraces carved into the fjord's gentle slopes, where the air smells of cut hay, woodsmoke, and the sweet tang of fermenting malt. The town stretches along a pebbled shore where fishing boats bob beside irrigation ditches, and goats and cattle wander lanes fenced with driftwood and whalebone. Its people are stocky, sun-browned, and uncommonly content, their cheeks red from labor and mead, and they speak with the unhurried drawl of folk who measure time by the harvest moon rather than the jarl's horn. Windbreaks of ancient birch and rowan, scarred with old harvest-runes, ring the settlement, and the drone of bees from the great mead-orchards is the town's constant music. Eyrby feeds Skaldvik and the fighting men of the north with grain, malt, and smoked meat, and its storehouses—thick-walled, thatched, and half-buried against the frost—hold enough to see Hrafnland through the harshest winter the frost giants have ever sent.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by Jarl Sigrid Barley-Mother, a hereditary chieftainess elected by the Thing of Eyrby and confirmed at the Althing. She holds her seat by the consent of the free farmers and owes the High Jarl of Hrafnland harvest-tithes and war-levies, but governs her fields and folk by ancient farming custom.
payload.terrain: Sheltered southern fjord valley with gentle slopes, pebbled shore, turf-roofed longhouses, and birch windbreaks

payload.summary: Where the northern coast of Hrafnland bends toward the frozen sea and the ice grinds against the shore for nine months of the year, Hvalhöfn clings to a wind-scoured headland of black basalt—a whaling station and walrus-camp that is less a town than a prolonged act of defiance against the cold. The settlement is a jumble of sod-walled shanties, whale-rib frames draped in oiled hides, and great iron cauldrons set over driftwood fires, their smoke reeking of rendered blubber so thickly that newcomers retch and old hands claim they can no longer smell it at all. Flensing racks line the shore, strung with strips of dark whale meat and slabs of blubber that cure in the bitter wind, and the beach is black with the bones of a thousand kills—ribs curving like cathedral arches, vertebrae the size of shields, and a jawbone arch that frames the harbor's entrance. The whalers themselves are a scarred, frost-bitten breed who speak little and sing less, and their skin boats, stretched over whalebone frames, put out into the ice floes with a recklessness that would be madness anywhere else. Hvalhöfn exports whale oil, walrus ivory, and narwhal horn to Skaldvik's traders, and the jarls of Hrafnland pay dearly for both, for the oil lights their halls and the ivory buys them ships and swords from the south.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by a Whaling-Captain elected annually from among the ship-masters at the Ice-Thing, a midwinter gathering held on the frozen strand. The Captain holds authority only during the hunt season; in the dark months, the camp's elder-hunters and the seidr-woman of the bone-circle share governance. The High Jarl's writ runs thin here, paid in oil and ivory rather than obedience.
payload.terrain: Wind-scoured basalt headland on the frozen northern coast, with sod shanties, flensing racks, whalebone arches, and ice-choked shore

payload.summary: On a wind-stripped moor where the frost heaves the earth into low, mossy mounds and a ring of standing stones juts from the bog like the broken teeth of a buried giant, Rúnarhólm is the rune-carvers' village of Hrafnland—a settlement of fewer than three hundred souls that is nonetheless revered across the nation as the keeper of its oldest memory. The village itself is a scatter of low, windowless stone bothies with turf roofs grown over with frost-tolerant heather, each built around a central hearth and sharing a wall with the next, so that the whole settlement forms a single wind-resistant ring with the standing stones at its heart. Every doorpost, lintel, and roof-beam is carved with runes—protective wards, lineage records, weather-prophecies, and the names of the dead—and the air carries the dry, mineral scent of freshly cut stone and the faint ozone tang of active seidr. The rune-carvers, men and women of the Rune-Guild, work the standing stones in slow rotation, recutting the ancient marks before the frost can wear them smooth, and their chanting carries across the moor at dawn and dusk in a low, droning harmony that the villagers say keeps the frost giants in their sleep. Few outsiders come to Rúnarhólm save those seeking a rune-wand, a naming-rune, or a doom-rune to lay on an enemy, and the carvers accept payment in iron, amber, or a true tale—never in mere silver.
payload.jurisdiction: Governed by the Rune-Guild's Master Carver, currently Thórvald Deep-Cut, who holds authority by mastery of the craft rather than blood, and who shares civil rule with the village's seidr-woman, the Volva Aldís Fog-Mother. The pair answer to the Althing in matters of law but hold the standing stones and their craft as sacred trust, above any jarl's command.
payload.terrain: Frost-heaved moor with mossy mounds, a ring of standing stones, and a ring of interconnected stone bothies with turf roofs

payload.summary: At the wide mouth of the Drekafjord where the greatest waterway of Hrafnland pours into the whale-road, Drekahöfn is the shipbuilding town of the nation—a long, roaring strand of boathouses, slipways, and tar-pits where the bones of Hrafnland's pride are shaped from oak, pine, and iron. The town straggles along a shelving beach of grey sand and driftwood, its timber yards stacked with cured planks that smell of pine resin and pitch, and the air is thick with the ring of adzes, the hiss of hot rivets quenched in seawater, and the bellowed work-chants of crews bending planks to frames. Longships in every stage of completion lean against the shore like sleeping dragons: bare keels propped on chocks, half-planked skeletons lashed with withes, and finished vessels freshly tarred and gleaming, their dragon-prows carved and painted and waiting for the sea. The shipwrights are a proud, secretive craft-guild who guard the lines and curves of their hulls as a smith guards his steel, and their master, the Ship-Builder Gísli Iron-Rivet, can judge a hull's speed from the hang of its strakes and has never launched a slow ship. Drekahöfn builds the warships that carry Hrafnland's raiders and the knarrs that carry its traders, and every keel laid on its shore is a promise that the nation's reach will not shrink.
payload.jurisdiction: Ruled by a Ship-Builder elected by the Shipwrights' Guild and confirmed by the High Jarl of Hrafnland, who holds the right to commission warships and whose writ is strong here, for the fleet is the nation's lifeblood. The current Ship-Builder, Gísli Iron-Rivets, governs the yards, settles labor disputes, and sets the launch-tithes paid to the Althing.
payload.terrain: Shelving beach at a great fjord's mouth, with timber yards, slipways, tar-pits, and boathouses along the strand

locations.name: The Hall of the High Jarl

payload.summary: On the highest ridge of Skaldvik, overlooking the harbor and the whale-road beyond, the Hall of the High Jarl is the seat of Hrafnland's power—a great timber longhouse of oak and pine, its roof ridge carved with a row of gilded raven-prow figureheads and its walls hung inside with shields, war-banners, and the captured prows of enemy ships. The hall is a hundred paces long, its central fire-pit running the length of the building, the smoke drifting up through a louvered roof-hole that makes the high beams a permanent, drifting haze. Benches line both walls, padded with furs and sea-cushions, and the high seat at the hall's western end is a carved throne of driftwood and whalebone where the High Jarl sits to hear petitions, settle feuds, and drink the first horn at every feast. The air is a permanent fug of woodsmoke, mead, roasting meat, and the salt-tang of sea-wet cloaks drying by the fire, and the hall is never empty—retainers sleep on the benches, oath-sworn guards stand at the doors, and skalds compete for a place by the fire where their verses will carry. When the Althing is not in session, the hall is where Hrafnland is ruled, by the jarl's word and the weight of his oath-men.
payload.jurisdiction: The seat of the High Jarl of Hrafnland, who holds sovereign authority over the nation between Althing sessions. The High Jarl's household, oath-sworn húskarlar, and skalds administer from the hall, and the jarl's word is law save where the Althing has spoken.
payload.terrain: Hilltop longhouse of oak and pine with a gilded raven-ridge roof, central fire-pit, shield-lined walls, and a whalebone high seat

payload.summary: On the quay-side of Skaldvik, its sign a carved longship hung above a door made from the actual stern-post of a wrecked knarr, the Salted Hull is the most famous mead-hall in Hrafnland—a sprawling, low-ceilinged tavern where traders, raiders, skalds, and foreign merchants gather to drink, deal, and swap the sagas of the season's voyaging. The hall is a single vast room of dark timber, its floor hard-packed earth strewn with rushes and salt, its walls hung with nets, harpoons, and the merchant-factors' tally-boards that serve as the tavern's unofficial ledger. A fire-pit at the center roasts whatever the kitchen has taken in trade—seal, whale, mutton, or the occasional strange fish from the southern seas—and the air is a dense, warm fog of mead-smoke, pine tar, wet wool, and the rich salt smell of the harbor outside. The mead, brewed in Eyrby and shipped in oak barrels, flows from a tapped cask behind the bar, and the barkeep—a one-armed former raider named Egil Wave-Cut—pours with a generosity that is matched only by his memory for unpaid tabs. A skald is always performing somewhere in the hall, and the competition for audience is fierce, for a skald who wins the Salted Hull's crowd has won Hrafnland's ear.
payload.jurisdiction: A private establishment licensed by the harbor-master of Skaldvik. Egil Wave-Cut, the proprietor, holds the license and enforces order with his remaining arm and the authority of a man who has killed more people than most of his patrons have met.
payload.terrain: Quay-side mead-hall with a wrecked-knarr door, earth floor, net-and-harpoon walls, a central fire-pit, and a tapped mead-cask bar

payload.summary: The Raven Quay is the great stone-and-timber harbor of Skaldvik, the busiest port in Hrafnland and the hinge on which the nation's trade with the wider world turns—a long, L-shaped stretch of piers, wharves, and warehouses where longships, knarrs, and foreign cogs jostle for berthing space and the air is a permanent cocktail of salt, tar, fish, and the sweet rot of wet timber. Stevedores in sea-boots haul bales of wool, barrels of whale oil, and crates of southern iron along the quays, while merchants shout prices in Norse, the southern tongue, and a dozen pidgins born of the trade-routes. Cranes of timber and rope swing cargo between dock and deck, and the harbor-master's tower at the quay's elbow flies a great black raven-banner that signals the port is open and the watch is set. Beneath the quays, in the salt-damp dark, smugglers move untaxed goods and stolen iron through passages that honeycomb the waterfront, and the harbor watch—six boats and a garrison of bored, bribable men—makes a show of policing what it cannot control. Every legal cargo in Hrafnland passes through the Raven Quay, and a good portion of the illegal cargo, too.
payload.jurisdiction: Administered by the Harbor-Master of Skaldvik, appointed by the High Jarl, who manages berthing, customs, and port defense. The harbor watch, a modest force, handles day-to-day enforcement, though its reach is famously limited where the smugglers are concerned.
payload.terrain: L-shaped harbor of stone and timber piers, wharves, warehouses, a harbor-master's tower, and smuggling passages beneath

locations.name: The Grove of the Nine Ravens

payload.summary: On a windswept point above the harbor where the land falls away to the sea and the wind is a constant, keening presence, the Grove of the Nine Ravens is Skaldvik's holiest ground—a ring of nine ancient yew trees, their branches twisted by centuries of salt wind into shapes that resemble nothing so much as the arms of drowned sailors reaching for the sky. At the grove's center stands a single runestone, waist-high and moss-dark, carved with the Nine-Raven sigil that gives the grove its name, and around it, driven into the earth at the base of each yew, are nine iron poles hung with offerings—twisted rag-charms, carved bone-tokens, locks of hair, and the occasional seidr-wand left by a volva whose magic was spent. The grove is tended by a single godhi, a grey-bearded priest named Hákon Tree-Eye, who lives in a sod hut at the grove's edge and who, it is whispered, has not left the point in thirty years. The air here smells of salt, yew resin, and the faint metallic tang of old blood from the blotr-sacrifices offered at the turning of the seasons, when the godhi bleeds a black ram and lets its blood run down the runestone to feed the land-wights. No iron is drawn in the grove, and no oath sworn there has ever been broken without the oath-breaker coming to a bad end—a reputation that keeps the grove feared and frequented in equal measure.
payload.jurisdiction: An independent sacred site tended by Godhi Hákon Tree-Eye, who holds sole authority over the grove and its rites. The High Jarl's writ does not extend within the grove's ring, by ancient compact, and even the Althing defers to the godhi in matters of the grove's sanctity.
payload.terrain: Windswept sea-point with a ring of nine twisted yew trees, a central moss-dark runestone, and nine iron offering-poles

payload.summary: In a stone-walled yard behind the quay, where the salt wind is broken by a screen of driftwood and whalebone, the Frostforge Smithy is Skaldvik's premier iron-works—a single, soot-blackened forge manned by a family of smiths who have worked the same anvil for six generations and who claim their first ancestor was taught by a dwarf in exchange for a night's hospitality. The smithy is open to the weather on three sides, its roof of turf and timber smoking with the heat of a furnace fed by charcoal shipped from the inland forests, and the ring of the master smith's hammer on the anvil is a sound the whole harbor knows. The smiths of the Frostforge work bog iron and southern bar-iron into the nails, rivets, axes, and ship-fittings that keep Hrafnland's fleet afloat, and their finest work—decorated axe-heads, inlaid seax-blades, and the rare iron war-helm—commands prices that only a jarl can pay. The master smith, a broad, burned woman named Ragnhild Coal-Hand, is said to know the secret of quenching steel in saltwater to give it a frost-blue edge, and she guards the secret as closely as a rune-carver guards his marks. The smithy smells of hot iron, coal smoke, and the sea, and its sparks fly out into the night like a constant, small constellation.
payload.jurisdiction: A private family workshop licensed by the High Jarl. Ragnhild Coal-Hand, the master smith, holds the license and governs the smithy as a family holding, answering to the jarl only in matters of war-levy and the supply of ship-fittings.
payload.terrain: Open-air stone-walled forge with a turf-and-timber roof, charcoal furnace, driftwood wind-screen, and a six-generation anvil

payload.summary: At the heart of Eyrby, its ridge-pole carved with sheaves of barley and its doorposts painted the red of ripe rowan, Jarl Sigrid Barley-Mother's longhouse is the seat of the southern farmland's rule—a broad, low hall of turf and timber built more for warmth than for war, its walls thick with sod and its roof a deep thatch of barley straw that turns gold in the summer sun. The hall is smaller and lower than the High Jarl's, but cozier: a single fire-pit warms the whole room, the smoke curling up through a roof-hole that has blackened the high beams to a glossy obsidian, and the benches are padded with sheepskin and barley-straw cushions that smell of dust and malt. The jarl's high seat is a carved chair of apple-wood, and beside it stands the Harvest-Horn, a great drinking-horn bound in silver, from which Sigrid toasts the first sheaf of every harvest and the last sheaf of every fall. The walls are hung not with shields but with farming tools—decorated sickles, a prized plow-share, and the great iron cauldron used for the harvest feast—and the air is a permanent, gentle fog of baking bread, malt-smoke, and the sweet, sleepy smell of hay. Here Sigrid holds the Thing of Eyrby, settles land-disputes, and hosts the harvest feasts that are the social highlight of the farming year.
payload.jurisdiction: The seat of Jarl Sigrid Barley-Mother, who governs Eyrby by the consent of the free farmers and the ancient farming custom. She holds the Thing of Eyrby in the longhouse, settles land-disputes, and presides over the harvest feasts, owing the High Jarl tithes and war-levies.
payload.terrain: Broad turf-and-timber longhouse with a barley-straw thatch, a single central fire-pit, an apple-wood high seat, and farming-tool-lined walls

payload.summary: On the sunny slope above the town, where the birch windbreak gives way to long, ordered rows of beehives and barley terraces, the Goldmalt Meadery is Eyrby's pride and Hrafnland's greatest mead-works—a cluster of low, turf-roofed malthouses and a single, larger brewing-hall whose chimneys trail a permanent sweet-smoke that the whole town knows as the smell of a good year. The meadery is run by the Mead-Guild, a family-craft order that has tended the same yeast-strain for nine generations and guards its malt-house secrets as fiercely as any rune-carver guards his marks. Inside the brewing-hall, great copper vats bubble over charcoal fires, and the air is a thick, humid fog of fermenting malt, honey, and the sharp, bright scent of brewer's herbs—juniper, bog-myrtle, and the wild thyme that grows only on the fjord's upper slopes. The master brewer, a white-haired, flour-dusted woman named Inga Goldmalt, can judge a mead's readiness by the sound of its ferment and has never released a bad barrel. The meadery's Goldmalt Mead is shipped to Skaldvik and from there to every hall in Hrafnland, and a jarl who cannot serve Goldmalt at his feast is a jarl whose guests will talk.
payload.jurisdiction: A family-craft workshop governed by the Mead-Guild and its master brewer, Inga Goldmalt. The guild holds a charter from Jarl Sigrid granting it exclusive right to brew mead for trade within Eyrby, and pays the jarl a tithe of every barrel shipped.
payload.terrain: Sunny slope with turf-roofed malthouses, a brewing-hall with copper vats, beehive rows, and barley terraces

payload.summary: Dug into the north-facing slope of the fjord's wall, where the frozen ground keeps the interior cold even in the height of summer, the Winter-Eye Granary is Eyrby's storehouse against famine—a half-buried complex of stone-walled, turf-roofed chambers linked by low, drafty passages, holding enough grain, smoked meat, and seed-stock to feed Hrafnland's south through two failed harvests. The granary's entrance is a single low door of iron-bound oak, flanked by two carved stone eyes—the 'winter-eyes' that give the place its name and that, the farmers believe, watch for the coming of the Fimbul-winter and the frost giants' last march. Inside, the air is cold, dry, and still, smelling of dust, dry grain, and the faint resin of the pine planks that line the storage bins. Sacks of barley, bins of seed-grain, and hanging rows of smoked mutton and salted fish are stacked in careful, inventory-ordered rows, and a granary-warden—a dour, precise man named Ólafur Dry-Hand—keeps a tally-board that is said to be more accurate than the jarl's own. The Winter-Eye is opened only by the jarl's seal and the warden's key, together, and in the lean years—when the frost comes early or the raiders burn the fields—what comes out of the Winter-Eye is the difference between Eyrby surviving and Eyrby becoming a saga of warning.
payload.jurisdiction: A communal storehouse under the joint seal of Jarl Sigrid and the granary-warden, Ólafur Dry-Hand, who is appointed by the Thing of Eyrby. Neither can open the granary alone; the warden controls the key and the jarl the seal, a balance designed to prevent abuse in lean years.
payload.terrain: Half-buried stone granary in a north-facing slope, with iron-bound oak doors, carved winter-eye stones, and turf-roofed storage chambers

payload.summary: On a level, grass-grown mound at the southern edge of town, where the windbreak of birch opens to the sky and the view sweeps the whole fjord-valley, the Thing-Mound of Eyrby is the open-air assembly-place where the free farmers of the south gather to make law, settle blood-feuds, and elect their jarl—a flat-topped barrow, ancient and grassed-over, ringed by a circle of standing boundary-stones each carved with the mark of a founding family. At the mound's center, a single flat stone—the Law-Stone—serves as the speaker's platform, and around it the farmers sit on the grass in concentric rings, their weapons stacked at the ring's edge by ancient custom, for no iron is drawn at the Thing. The Law-Speaker, a memory-trained elder who knows the farming-custom by heart, recites the law at the opening of each assembly, and his voice carries across the mound in the still air of the late summer morning. The mound is used only for the Thing and for the harvest-home blessing, and for the rest of the year it is left to the grass and the land-wights, but every farmer in Eyrby knows its contours as well as his own field, for the law made here is the law he lives by.
payload.jurisdiction: Sacred assembly-ground under the authority of the Thing of Eyrby, the free farmers' assembly. The Law-Speaker, an elected elder, recites and interprets the customary law. The mound is neutral ground where the jarl's seal is not recognized and no iron may be drawn.
payload.terrain: Flat-topped grass-grown barrow ringed by carved boundary-stones, with a central Law-Stone speaker's platform, on a level mound at the valley's edge

payload.summary: The black-sand shore below the headland, where the whalers drag their kills and the air is a thick, greasy fog of blood and rendered fat, the Flensing Strand is Hvalhöfn's works-floor—the place where the whale becomes the goods that keep the station alive. Great iron cauldrons sit over driftwood fires along the tide-line, their contents bubbling to clear oil that is skimmed into barrels and rolled up the headland by hand, and the beach itself is a slick, trampled field of blubber-scraps, bone-shards, and the dark, tarry residue of a thousand renderings. Flensing racks of whalebone and timber line the upper strand, strung with strips of meat and slabs of blubber that cure in the bitter wind, and the whalers work the carcasses with long, curved flensing-knives in a slow, skilled dance that strips a whale to the bone in a single tide. The gulls are a constant, screaming cloud above the strand, and the station's dogs—shaggy, yellow-eyed beasts bred to guard the meat from the birds and the bears—patrol the racks with a territorial snarl. The strand is the hardest, ugliest, most essential place in Hvalhöfn, and the men and women who work it are paid in oil-shares and the grim pride of a job that the nation cannot do without.
payload.jurisdiction: A communal works-floor managed by the Whaling-Captain during hunt season and by the elder-hunters in the dark months. Labor on the strand is organized by oil-shares—a worker's portion of the rendered oil is proportional to the flensing-shifts worked—and disputes are settled by the elder-hunters' council.
payload.terrain: Black-sand shore with iron rendering-cauldrons over driftwood fires, whalebone flensing racks, a trampled slick of blubber and bone, and a constant cloud of gulls

payload.summary: On the wind-scoured crest of the headland, where the ice-wind is strongest and the view sweeps the frozen sea to the edge of sight, the Bone-Circle is the seidr-ground of Hvalhöfn—a ring of standing whale-ribs, each as tall as a man and driven point-down into the frozen earth, their curved upper ends meeting to form a low, dome-like arch that the wind sings through with a sound the whalers call the Ice-Volva's breath. Within the ring, the ground is bare, black, and frozen hard, scattered with the bones of seals, walrus, and the occasional narwhal, and at the center stands a single flat stone—the doom-stone—where the station's seidr-woman, the Volva Mörgrím Ice-Bone, casts the runes and reads the whale-hunt's luck before every putting-out. Mörgrím is a tall, gaunt, white-haired woman of uncertain age who wears a cloak of sewn-together seal-skins and who is said to have survived three days naked in the ice as a test of her calling, and her eyes are the pale, washed-out blue of the midwinter sky. The air in the bone-circle is always colder than the surrounding headland, and the whalers cross themselves—old habit, old faith—when they pass it, for the seidr worked here is the old, dark kind, the kind that speaks to the dead and the deep things under the ice, and the volva's word on whether a hunt is cursed or blessed is the word that decides whether the boats put out or stay.
payload.jurisdiction: An independent seidr-ground tended by the Volva Mörgrím Ice-Bone, whose authority in matters of hunt-luck, curse-lifting, and the dead is absolute and unquestioned by the whalers. The Whaling-Captain defers to the volva on whether a hunt is blessed or cursed, and the elder-hunters' council does not overrule her.
payload.terrain: Wind-scoured headland crest with a ring of standing whale-ribs forming a low dome, a bare frozen floor scattered with sea-bones, and a central doom-stone

payload.summary: At the headland's lee, where a natural shelf of basalt breaks the wind and the spray, the Skin-Boat Sheds are Hvalhöfn's harbor—a row of low, driftwood-framed shelters, each roofed with oiled hides and each holding a single skin-boat, the whalers' fragile, deadly craft that are to Hvalhöfn what longships are to Skaldvik. The boats are built over whalebone frames, their skins of sewn seal-hide stretched tight and oiled to a dark, supple finish that gleams when wet, and they are light enough for two men to carry but strong enough to ride the ice-floe swells where a timber boat would be stove in. Each shed is marked with its boat's name—Whale-Bane, Ice-Biter, Cold-Sister—and a carved figurehead on the shed's lintel that the whalers touch for luck before every putting-out. The sheds smell of seal-oil, wet hide, and the faint, sharp scent of the pine-pitch used to seal the seams, and the boat-builders—a small, specialized crew who work only in the dark months when the boats are ashore—can re-skin a boat in three days and would stake their oil-shares on every stitch. The skin-boats are Hvalhöfn's lifeline, and a boat-builder is a more important man than a whaling-captain, for without the boats there is no hunt.
payload.jurisdiction: Communal harbor sheds managed by the elder-hunters' council, which assigns shed-space by hunt-seniority. The boat-builders, a specialized crew, hold a charter from the Ice-Thing granting them exclusive right to build and re-skin the station's boats, and their work is paid in oil-shares.
payload.terrain: Basalt shelf at the headland's lee, with driftwood-framed hide-roofed sheds holding skin-boats over whalebone frames, marked by carved figureheads

payload.summary: Clustered behind the headland's crest, where the wind carries the smoke away from the living-shanties, the Black-Smoke Houses are Hvalhöfn's curing-works—a tight cluster of low, stone-walled, turf-roofed smoke-shacks whose chimneys trail a perpetual, dense, grey-black smoke that reeks of peat, blubber, and cured meat and that can be smelled from a mile downwind. Inside, the shacks are divided into hanging-chambers where strips of whale meat, slabs of seal, and the occasional walrus-side hang from rafters of whalebone and driftwood, cured slowly over smoldering peat fires tended by the station's curers—a dour, smoke-blackened crew who judge a cure by touch and smell and who would never eat meat they hadn't cured themselves. The floors are a greasy, ash-scattered mess, and the heat is dry, close, and eye-watering, but the output—dark, salt-rubbed, smoke-cured meat that can keep for two winters without spoiling—is Hvalhöfn's second great export after oil, and the jarls of Hrafnland pay in iron and amber for the chests of black-smoke meat that ship out on every trader. The master curer, a silent, soot-stained man named Björn Ash-Hand, has cured meat on this headland for forty years and claims he can still taste the first whale he ever smoked.
payload.jurisdiction: Communal curing-works managed by the elder-hunters' council. The master curer, Björn Ash-Hand, holds a charter from the Ice-Thing granting him authority over the smoke-houses and the cure-schedules, and curers are paid in oil-shares and a share of the cured meat.
payload.terrain: Cluster of stone-walled, turf-roofed smoke-shacks behind the headland, with hanging-chambers of whalebone rafters, peat fires, and ash-scattered floors

locations.name: The Ring of the First Runes

payload.summary: At the moor's heart, where the frost-heave has pushed the earth into a low, uneven dome and the moss grows thick and grey-green over stone older than memory, the Ring of the First Runes is Rúnarhólm's holiest ground and the reason the village exists at all—a circle of twenty-four standing stones, each taller than a man, each carved from top to bottom with runes so old that even the Master Carver admits he does not read them all. The stones are not uniform: some are rough-hewn granite, dark with lichen; others are pale, almost white, a stone found nowhere else in Hrafnland and said to have been carried by the first rune-carvers from a quarry now lost under the ice. The runes themselves are cut deep, recut every generation by the Rune-Guild to keep the frost from wearing them smooth, and at dawn and dusk the carvers walk the ring in slow procession, chanting the rune-names in a droning harmony that the villagers say holds the frost giants in their sleep beneath the moor. The air in the ring is still, colder than the surrounding moor, and charged with a faint, persistent hum that sets the teeth aching and the small hairs of the arms rising—a hum the carvers call 'the stone-singing' and that no seidr-woman has fully explained. No one stands in the ring's center after dark, not even the Master Carver, for the stones are said to wake when the light is gone, and what they wake as is a thing the old sagas do not name.
payload.jurisdiction: Sacred ground under the sole authority of the Rune-Guild and its Master Carver, Thórvald Deep-Cut. No civil or jarl's writ runs within the ring; even the Althing defers to the Guild in matters of the stones' care, recutting, and access, which is granted only to Guild members and those they explicitly permit.
payload.terrain: Frost-heaved moor-dome with a circle of twenty-four standing stones of granite and pale white stone, deeply carved with ancient runes, ringed by grey-green moss

payload.summary: The interconnected ring of low, windowless stone bothies that forms the village proper is less a settlement than a single building shaped like a broken ring around the standing stones—each bothy sharing a wall with its neighbors, each roofed with turf grown over with frost-heather, and each connected to the next by a low, drafty passage that lets a carver walk the whole village without stepping outside. The bothies are the homes and workshops of the Rune-Guild's members, and every interior surface—doorposts, lintels, roof-beams, even the stone headrests of the sleeping-benches—is carved with runes: protective wards above the doors, lineage-records on the bed-posts, weather-prophecies on the hearth-lintels, and the names of the dead on the memorial-stones set into the floors. The air is a permanent, dry, mineral scent of fresh-cut stone and the faint ozone of active seidr, and the sound of chisel on stone is the village's constant, quiet music, audible through the shared walls at all hours. Each bothy has a single hearth, a single sleeping-bench, and a work-table strewn with chisels, rune-punches, and the small, meticulous tools of the carver's craft, and the carvers themselves—men and women of quiet, focused intensity—work in a concentration so deep that a visitor can stand in the doorway unremarked for a quarter-hour before being noticed.
payload.jurisdiction: The bothies are the homes and workshops of the Rune-Guild's members, allocated by the Master Carver according to guild seniority. Civil disputes within the bothies are settled by the Master Carver and the Volva Aldís jointly, and the Althing's writ is recognized only in matters of blood and theft.
payload.terrain: Interconnected ring of windowless stone bothies with turf roofs, shared walls, interior passages, rune-carved surfaces, and single-hearth workshops

payload.summary: Set apart from the bothy-ring, on a low mound at the moor's edge where the fog gathers first and lingers longest, the Fog-Mother's Hut is the dwelling and seidr-ground of the Volva Aldís Fog-Mother, Rúnarhólm's seidr-woman and the village's co-ruler—a low, round, turf-roofed hut whose walls are of stacked stone and whose only door faces north, toward the ice, and is hung with a curtain of grey woven wool that is never fully still, even when the wind is calm. Inside, the hut is a single, dim, smoke-hazed room: a central hearth whose fire is never allowed to go out, a sleeping-platform covered in furs, and a seidr-platform of raised earth where Aldís sits on a whalebone seat—the high-seat—and enters the seidr-trance that lets her see what is hidden, what is coming, and what the stones have said. The air smells of woodsmoke, dried herbs—yarrow, mugwort, and the frostwort that grows only on the moor—and the faint, cold, electric scent of active seidr. Aldís herself is small, old, and wrapped in layers of grey wool and fox-fur, her white hair braided with bone-beads and her eyes the pale, distant grey of the moor-fog she is named for. She speaks little, and what she speaks is delivered in a low, even voice that the villagers treat as law, for the Fog-Mother's word on a birth, a death, or a doom-rune is the word that the village lives by, and even the Master Carver, who rules the craft, defers to her in matters of the unseen.
payload.jurisdiction: The independent dwelling and seidr-ground of the Volva Aldís Fog-Mother, who shares civil rule with the Master Carver and holds sole authority over seidr-matters, divination, birth and death-omens, and the laying of doom-runes. Her word on the unseen is not overruled by any authority in the village.
payload.terrain: Low round turf-roofed hut on a foggy moor-edge mound, with a single north door, a perpetual central hearth, a whalebone seidr high-seat, and herb-hung walls

payload.summary: The single track that climbs the moor from the southern lowlands, a causeway of flat stones laid over the bog where the frost-heave is worst, the Amber-Iron Road is Rúnarhólm's only link to the wider world and the route by which the village's rune-work goes out and its payment comes in. The road is narrow, winding, and impassable for carts—everything that moves along it moves on a man's back or a pack-pony's—and it is marked at every turning by a rune-stone, a waist-high way-marker carved with a directional rune and the distance to the next stone, which the carvers maintain as part of their sacred duty. At the road's moor-end, where it meets the bothy-ring, a single open-faced trading-stone—a flat-topped boulder polished smooth by generations of laid-out wares—serves as the village's market, where the carvers display their rune-wands, naming-runes, and protective wards for the traders and petitioners who make the climb. Payment is never in silver alone: the carvers take iron, amber, true tales, and, for the greatest work, a sworn oath, and the traders who come up the road are a specialized breed—tough, laconic, and unfailingly respectful of the stones and the carvers, for a man who insults the Rune-Guild does not get a second carven word from them. The road is closed by snow for half the year, and in that time the village is alone with the moor and the stones and the fog.
payload.jurisdiction: The road and trading-stone are maintained by the Rune-Guild as a sacred trust; the way-marker stones are recut by the Guild as part of their duties. Trade at the trading-stone is overseen by the Master Carver, who sets the prices for rune-work and adjudicates disputes with traders.
payload.terrain: Narrow stone causeway over boggy moor, marked by waist-high rune way-stones, ending at a flat polished trading-boulder at the bothy-ring's edge

payload.summary: The heart of Drekahöfn, a wide, shelving stretch of grey sand and timber shoring where the slipways run down to the waterline and the air rings with the adze and the rivet-hammer, the Longkeel Shipyard is where Hrafnland's longships are born—the greatest shipbuilding yard in the nation and the source of the fleet that carries the raiders to the whale-road and the traders to the south. The yard holds six slipways, each a cradle of timber shoring and wedge-blocks where a hull is built keel-up and then levered, with the whole town's muscle, to be rolled on logs into the sea. A keel-laying draws every shipwright in the yard, and the laying of a warship's keel is a rite overseen by the Ship-Builder himself, who drives the first rivet with a silver hammer that is then locked away until the next. The yard's timber yards, stacked with cured pine and oak planks that smell of resin and pitch, flank the slipways, and the tar-pits—a row of smoking, bubbling cauldrons where hull-planks are dipped before fitting—trail a permanent, acrid haze that the town breathes without noticing. The shipwrights work in crews of six to a slipway, each crew's master a grey-bearded veteran who knows every line of the hull by touch, and the yard's output—three to five longships a year, and twice as many knarrs—is the measure of Hrafnland's reach.
payload.jurisdiction: The shipyard is the seat of the Ship-Builder's authority, governed by Gísli Iron-Rivets and the Shipwrights' Guild. The Guild allocates slipways, settles labor disputes, and sets the launch-tithes paid to the Althing. The High Jarl holds the right to commission warships and prioritizes the yard's warship capacity.
payload.terrain: Wide shelving grey-sand strand with six timber-shored slipways, stacked timber yards, smoking tar-pits, and log-rolling launch ways

payload.summary: A long, open-fronted shed at the shipyard's western end, where the wind carries off the shavings and the light is good for fine carving, the Dragon-Prow Works is the workshop of Drekahöfn's carvers—the specialists who shape the figureheads that give Hrafnland's longships their name and their terror. The shed is strewn with wood-shavings to the ankle, its benches lined with half-finished prows in pine and oak: dragons with gilded teeth, ravens with spread wings, serpents coiled to strike, and the occasional wolf's-head for a jarl's personal ship. The master carver, a lean, quiet, long-fingered man named Leif Dragon-Cut, can spend a month on a single prow and has never shipped one he did not consider worthy, and his work commands a price second only to the hull itself. The air smells of fresh-cut pine, pine-tar, and the faint mineral scent of the gilding-leaf that the carvers apply to teeth, eyes, and wing-tips, and the shed's back wall is hung with the carved eyes—gilded, painted, or set with amber—that are the last piece fitted before a ship is launched. A ship's prow is its luck, the raiders say, and a ship that puts to sea with a botched prow is a ship that will not come home, so the carvers are honored as highly as the shipwrights and paid in silver, iron, and a share of the raid-spoil when the ship returns.
payload.jurisdiction: A specialist workshop within the Shipwrights' Guild, governed by Master Carver Leif Dragon-Cut under the Ship-Builder's overall authority. The carvers hold an independent charter within the Guild to set figurehead prices and to refuse commissions they deem beneath their craft.
payload.terrain: Open-fronted pine-shaving-strewn shed at the shipyard's west end, with carving benches, half-finished figureheads, a gilding-leaf back wall, and amber prow-eyes

payload.summary: At the inland edge of town, where the forest begins and the air is a permanent, eye-stinging fog of woodsmoke and pine-resin, the Black-Pit Tar-Works is Drekahöfn's tar-mill—the operation that produces the pitch and tar that waterproof every hull, every seam, and every rope in Hrafnland's fleet. The works is a cluster of tar-pits—deep, stone-lined trenches roofed with turf and stacked with pine root-wood that is burned slow and airless, dripping a thick, black, acrid tar into collection-troughs at the pit's base—and the air for a quarter-mile downwind is heavy with the smell, which the tar-workers no longer notice and which every visitor never forgets. The tar-master, a black-stained, bandy-legged man named Grímmur Black-Pit, runs the works with a crew of a dozen who tend the slow fires day and night in shifts, judging the burn by the color of the smoke and the smell of the drip, and who are paid in silver and a share of every barrel shipped. The tar is barrelled, rolled to the shipyard, and applied hot to every plank-seam and rope-fiber before a ship puts out, and a shipwright will not launch a hull whose tar is not Grímmur's, for a seam that leaks is a seam that sinks, and the Black-Pit tar has never leaked in living memory. The works also produces the pine-pitch used for torches and the resin used for the carvers' gilding, and its fires have not been fully out in three generations.
payload.jurisdiction: A private chartered works under the tar-master Grímmur Black-Pit, who holds a charter from the Ship-Builder granting him exclusive right to produce ship-tar for the yard. The Shipwrights' Guild regulates tar quality and sets the barrel-price, and the tar-workers are paid in silver and tar-shares.
payload.terrain: Inland forest-edge cluster of stone-lined turf-roofed tar-pits with slow airless fires, collection-troughs, and a permanent acrid smoke-fog

payload.summary: On a low rise above the slipways, its ridge-pole carved with a row of miniature dragon-prows and its doorposts shaped like the stems of a longship, the Ship-Builder's Hall is the seat of Drekahöfn's rule and the social heart of the shipbuilding town—a long, high-roofed timber hall that is half longhouse, half guildhall, built to house the Ship-Builder's household, host the Shipwrights' Guild meetings, and feed the yard's crews at the launch-feasts that are the town's great occasion. The hall's central fire-pit runs two-thirds of its length, and the high seat at the western end is a carved chair whose arms are shaped from the curved stem-pieces of the first longship Gísli Iron-Rivets ever built, a trophy and a throne in one. The walls are hung with the shipwrights' tools—decorated adzes, rivet-hammers, and the great two-man crosscut saws that shape the keel-timbers—and with the painted launch-banners of every ship built in the yard, a record of the fleet that makes the hall feel less like a dwelling than like a gallery of the nation's sea-power. The air is a warm, workmanlike fug of woodsmoke, mead, pine-tar, and the sweat of shipwrights celebrating a launch, and at a launch-feast the hall is packed stem to stern with the whole town, drinking, boasting, and singing the work-chants of the yard until the high beams ring.
payload.jurisdiction: The seat of the Ship-Builder Gísli Iron-Rivets, who governs Drekahöfn under the High Jarl's commission. The hall also serves as the meeting-place of the Shipwrights' Guild, where the Guild's inner council sets slipway allocations, labor terms, and launch-tithes, and where the Ship-Builder adjudicates disputes.
payload.terrain: Long high-roofed timber hall on a rise above the slipways, with a long central fire-pit, a stem-piece high seat, tool-and-banner-lined walls, and a launch-feast capacity

payload.summary: A stone-walled, soot-blackened forge at the shipyard's eastern edge, set apart from the timber works by a firewall of stacked sod and open to the sea-wind on three sides for the draft, the Anchor-Iron Forge is Drekahöfn's iron-works—the forge that produces the rivets, nails, anchors, and iron-fittings that hold Hrafnland's ships together. The forge is run by a family of ship-smiths who have worked the same anvil for four generations and who supply the yard exclusively, and its master, a huge, softly-spoken man named Hákon Anchor-Hand, can judge a rivet's heat by the color of the glow and has never shipped a soft nail. The forge works bog iron and southern bar-iron, smelted in a charcoal furnace whose chimney trails a permanent grey plume over the eastern strand, and the ring of Hákon's trip-hammer on the anvil is the yard's clock, audible across the whole town. The rivets are the ship's bones—a longship holds thousands, each hand-forged, each quenched in saltwater for the frost-blue hardness the raiders trust—and the anchors are the ship's safety, great iron hooks that can hold a dragon-prowed longship in a gale. The forge smells of hot iron, coal smoke, and the sea, and its sparks fly out over the water at night like a second, lower constellation beneath the real one.
payload.jurisdiction: A family-chartered forge supplying the shipyard exclusively, governed by Master Smith Hákon Anchor-Hand under the Ship-Builder's authority. The forge holds a Guild charter to produce all ship-iron for the yard, and the ship-smiths are paid in silver and a share of every launch.
payload.terrain: Stone-walled soot-blackened forge at the yard's east edge, open to the sea-wind on three sides, with a charcoal furnace, a trip-hammer anvil, and a sod firewall
